hints: Focus on the gas first, what common gas turns red litmus paper blue?
Remember that this alkaline gas only comes from an ammonium salt like $\text{NH}_4\text{NO}_3$ when $\text{OH}^-$ ions are present to react with $\text{NH}_4^+$.
Ask yourself which of the four solids will dissolve to give a basic, $\text{OH}^-$-rich solution on heating.
walkthrough:
**Identify the mystery gas**

Great start, let's read the test result. A gas that turns red litmus to blue is alkaline.

In AS Chemistry this is almost always ammonia, $\text{NH}_3$.

**Recall how ammonia is released**

Ammonium ions only give off ammonia when warmed with a base, a source of hydroxide ions.

The key ionic equation is:
$$\text{NH}_4^+ + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Check what R does in water**

So R must create $\text{OH}^-$ ions in solution. Let's think about acid-base character:

$\text{Na}_2\text{O}$ is a basic Group 1 oxide: $\text{Na}_2\text{O} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{NaOH}$, strongly alkaline.

**Rule out the acidic solids**

$\text{AlCl}_3$ gives an acidic solution by hydrolysis, $\text{MgCl}_2$ is neutral to slightly acidic, and phosphorus oxide ($\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$) gives acidic phosphoric acid. None supply $\text{OH}^-$.

Only the basic oxide can drive the reaction to release $\text{NH}_3$.

options.A: Aluminium chloride hydrolyses in water to give an acidic solution containing $\text{H}^+$ and $[\text{Al}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_5(\text{OH})]^{2+}$. It cannot supply $\text{OH}^-$ to convert $\text{NH}_4^+$ to $\text{NH}_3$, so no ammonia is evolved.
options.B: Magnesium chloride dissolves to give a neutral to very weakly acidic solution. It provides $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ and $\text{Cl}^-$ ions, not $\text{OH}^-$ ions, so it will not displace $\text{NH}_3$ from ammonium nitrate.
options.C: Sodium oxide is strongly basic. It reacts with water to form sodium hydroxide: $\text{Na}_2\text{O} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{NaOH}$. On heating, $\text{OH}^-$ reacts: $\text{NH}_4^+ + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$, giving ammonia which turns red litmus blue.
options.D: Phosphorus oxide (e.g. $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$) is an acidic oxide. It dissolves to form phosphoric acid, $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$. Adding acid to $\text{NH}_4^+$ keeps ammonium protonated and prevents $\text{NH}_3$ release.
